items.h: Financial adviser office signs that feel discreet
items.p: Clients discussing pensions, investments or inheritance may prefer a discreet setting. Financial adviser office signs can identify the practice clearly without drawing unnecessary attention, using plaques, cut lettering or a neat name panel by the door. Any regulatory wording you need to display should come from your compliance team, and we will present it consistently.

Accountancy practice signage on building directories, in lift lobbies and on suite doors helps clients find you without phoning for directions. items.h: Accountant reception signs that welcome clients
items.p: Clients often arrive with paperwork and questions, and a calm reception sets the tone. Accountant reception signs can include your logo on the wall, directions to meeting rooms and a clear place to wait. Privacy graphics on glass meeting rooms help clients feel comfortable discussing their finances while keeping the office light.

items.h: Consultancy office signs for client visits
items.p: Consultancies often host workshops and client meetings, and the space should feel professional and organised. Consultancy office signs can identify the business at the entrance and label meeting rooms clearly, with names that are easy to quote in calendar invitations. A consistent style across rooms helps visitors move around confidently.

items.h: Agency reception signage and logo walls
items.p: For creative businesses, reception is a chance to show personality. Agency reception signage might use cut lettering, layered panels or printed graphics that reflect your brand voice. Think about how it looks in photographs too, as reception walls often appear in social posts, recruitment content and team pictures taken by visitors.

items.h: Office wall graphics for culture and work
items.p: Large walls in studios or breakout areas can carry values, project highlights or simply bold colour. Office wall graphics can be printed or cut to suit the surface, and replaced as the business changes. Linking them with the portable materials you use for pitches and events keeps your brand consistent inside and outside the office.

/sectors/offices/corporate-offices.lead: Corporate office signage has to carry a brand consistently across floors, departments and sometimes several buildings, while staying flexible enough to handle reorganisations and new teams.
/sectors/offices/corporate-offices.heading: Corporate office signage across floors and teams

items.h: Corporate reception signs that follow brand guidelines
items.p: The reception is often the most visible part of a corporate office for clients, candidates and partners. Corporate reception signs should follow brand guidelines closely, using approved logos, colours and typefaces. Share your guidelines at the start and we will design within them, flagging any detail that may not reproduce well at a larger scale.

items.h: Office meeting room signs that stay up to date
items.p: Meeting rooms are renamed, repurposed and rebooked constantly. Office meeting room signs with replaceable inserts or simple panels let facilities teams update names without contacting a supplier each time. Matching room names to the booking system avoids the familiar confusion of a calendar invite pointing to a room nobody can find.

items.h: Corporate wall graphics for shared spaces
items.p: Breakout areas, corridors and kitchens offer space to communicate values, history or purpose. Corporate wall graphics can turn plain walls into something that supports the culture while still feeling part of the same brand as reception. Plan these alongside wayfinding, so walls are not overloaded with competing messages and signs.

/sectors/offices/coworking.lead: Coworking space signage has to promote the building's own brand while making room for members and tenants who come and go, so flexibility matters as much as the look on day one.
/sectors/offices/coworking.heading: Coworking space signage that adapts to occupancy

items.h: Serviced office signage and tenant directories
items.p: Serviced offices often have many tenants on short agreements. Serviced office signage can include an entrance directory and suite door signs with replaceable name panels, so updates are quick and simple. Decide who manages changes and keep a master list, so the directory always reflects who is actually in the building.

items.h: Coworking wayfinding signs for shared facilities
items.p: Members need to find meeting rooms, phone booths, kitchens and quiet areas, often on their first day. Coworking wayfinding signs with consistent icons and names help them settle in without asking staff. Matching room names to the booking app or website keeps everything joined up for members and their visiting guests.

items.h: Shared office signage for small business suites
items.p: Small companies sharing a floor still want visitors to find them easily. Shared office signage can give each business a consistent door sign or panel in a format the building controls, avoiding a mix of homemade notices. That keeps corridors tidy and gives every tenant a professional presence from the day they move in.

/sectors/offices/coworking.close: Running a coworking or serviced office building? Get in touch about coworking space signage that is simple to keep current as members and tenants change.

/sectors/offices/solicitors.lead: Solicitor office signage should be discreet and professional, helping clients reach the right reception and meeting room while keeping names, matters and sensitive conversations out of public view.
/sectors/offices/solicitors.heading: Solicitor office signage that respects confidentiality

items.h: Law firm signage for multi-office practices
items.p: Firms with several offices across Norfolk and beyond want each to feel like the same practice. Law firm signage built from a consistent template, with fixed proportions for the name, logo and any accreditation artwork you supply, makes that straightforward. Each office can then be adapted to its building without the brand drifting over time.

items.h: Legal practice signs for period and town centre buildings
items.p: Many practices occupy older town centre buildings where a large fascia would look out of place. Legal practice signs such as engraved plaques, cut lettering or neat panels by the door can identify the firm in keeping with the building. Check any restrictions on listed or conservation-area properties before agreeing a design.

items.h: Solicitor reception signage and meeting rooms
items.p: Clients often arrive anxious about a legal matter. Solicitor reception signage can provide a calm welcome, clear directions to meeting rooms and nothing that reveals other clients' business. Privacy graphics on glazed meeting rooms, and room names rather than staff names, help keep conversations confidential and make the office feel composed.

/sectors/retail.lead: Retail shop signage has to tell shoppers what you sell before they reach the door, then help them find their way around once inside, while leaving room for offers that change.
/sectors/retail.heading: Retail shop signage from street to till

items.h: Shopfront signs that tell people what you sell
items.p: A name alone does not always explain the business. Shopfront signs that combine the name with a short descriptor, such as the product range or speciality, help passers-by decide to step inside. Our guide to measuring a fascia explains what to record so we can design to the right proportions.

items.h: Retail window graphics that support displays
items.p: Window displays sell products, so graphics should support them rather than compete. Retail window graphics can carry opening hours, social handles or a short brand message along the edges or lower part of the glass. Keep seasonal promotions on removable vinyl or poster frames, so the window can be refreshed regularly.

items.h: Retail store signage for departments and tills
items.p: Larger shops and showrooms need customers to find departments, fitting rooms, collection points and tills. Retail store signage can use hanging signs, wall graphics or freestanding panels in a consistent style. Planning with your floor plan puts signs where shoppers make decisions, rather than wherever wall space happens to be free.

/sectors/retail.close: From a single shop to several branches, talk to us about retail shop signage that suits your products, your premises and the way customers shop.

/sectors/retail/food-retailers.lead: Food shop signage should tell passers-by what you do best, whether that is bread, cheese, meat or local produce, while keeping daily prices and offers easy to change.

items.h: Bakery shop signs that catch early customers
items.p: Bakeries often open early and rely on commuters and regulars deciding quickly. Bakery shop signs should show the name and speciality clearly from a distance, with opening times visible on the door. A-boards or window panels for daily specials help catch people who might otherwise walk straight past on the way to work.

items.h: Food retailer signage for delis and farm shops
items.p: Delis, butchers, greengrocers and farm shops each have a different character to express. Food retailer signage can draw on that, using colours and lettering that suit the produce and the building. Labels, shelf signs and counter signs inside can follow the same style, so the shop feels coherent from the fascia to the till.

items.h: Food shop window graphics around displays
items.p: Food displays in windows are powerful, but they need to stay visible and fresh. Food shop window graphics can sit around the display, showing your name, opening hours and collection or ordering information. Keep changing prices and offers on a separate frame or board, so updates through the week do not involve new vinyl.

items.h: Plant nursery signs for growers and smaller sites
items.p: Nurseries and specialist growers often sit on rural lanes with little passing trade. Plant nursery signs at the road need clear names and opening days that can be read from a car. On site, simple bed and greenhouse labels help visitors browse independently, which matters when staff are busy potting up or serving.

items.h: Garden centre wayfinding signs between departments
items.p: Large centres combine plants, furniture, gifts, cafés and sometimes pet or aquatic areas. Garden centre wayfinding signs using consistent colours and names help shoppers move between these zones and find the tills. Signs in exposed outdoor areas need tougher materials and fixings than those in sheltered retail spaces under cover.

items.h: Garden centre entrance signs for car parks
items.p: The entrance and car park set the tone for the visit and help manage busy weekends. Garden centre entrance signs can welcome visitors, show opening hours and point to trolley bays, the café or collection points. Making the main entrance obvious from the car park also stops shoppers wandering into delivery areas.

items.h: Kitchen showroom signs and display labels
items.p: Kitchen customers often compare several showrooms before deciding. Kitchen showroom signs at the entrance and on each display can name ranges, finishes or styles, helping customers remember what they liked. Keep display labels in a consistent, replaceable format, so ranges can change without disturbing the overall look of the showroom.

items.h: Bathroom showroom signage for compact layouts
items.p: Bathroom displays are often smaller and closer together, so signs need to be readable without crowding the room sets. Bathroom showroom signage might use small wall panels, freestanding stands or graphics on display walls. Agree which details customers need at each display, such as range names or features, and keep pricing on a separate card that is easy to update.

items.h: Showroom display graphics that suggest a lifestyle
items.p: Large images of finished rooms help customers imagine how products will look at home. Showroom display graphics can be printed for walls, panels or hanging banners, and updated as ranges change. Linking them to the exterior branding keeps the showroom feeling coherent from the car park to the design desk where orders are discussed.

/sectors/retail/independent-shops.heading: Independent shop signage with personality

items.h: Small shop signs for a narrow frontage
items.p: Many independents occupy small units with a narrow fascia and a single window. Small shop signs need careful proportion, so the name is readable without crowding the door or display. A projecting sign or a well-designed A-board can extend visibility along the street, especially in lanes and arcades where people approach from the side.

items.h: Shop fascia signs that suit the building
items.p: Older high streets and market towns often have character buildings and, in some areas, conservation rules. Shop fascia signs should respect the proportions of the building while showing your brand clearly. Painted-style lettering, raised letters or a simple panel can each suit different frontages, and checking local requirements early avoids redesigns.

items.h: Shop window lettering for hours and services
items.p: Window lettering is a simple way to add information and character. Shop window lettering can show opening hours, social handles, services or a short description of what you sell. Keep it to a small area of the glass, so the display remains the star and the shop does not look cluttered from the pavement.

items.p: Leisure centre visitors range from regular swimmers to families on a first visit. items.h: Entertainment venue signs that build anticipation
items.p: Bowling alleys, escape rooms, cinemas and gaming venues sell an experience. items.p: Clubs and stadiums need to direct home fans, away supporters, players, officials and hospitality guests along different routes. items.p: Guests at hotels and guest houses notice signs most when they are trying to find check-in or their room.
